ICILS employed a two-stage cluster sample (schools sampled with probability proportional to enrollment, then students sampled within schools; teachers sampled within schools), and the report states that sampling weights and nonresponse adjustments were calculated for each country to produce final weights for each sampled unit. All findings presented in the report are based on appropriately weighted data, but the specific weight variable name is not provided in the excerpt. Replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not described here, so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This chapter uses ICILS 2013 grade eight student computer-based assessment of computer and information literacy (CIL) plus a student questionnaire administered after the test. Students completed two randomly allocated 30-minute test modules from four, yielding one-hour total assessment time, and CIL achievement was scaled on a metric with mean 500 and SD 100 using Rasch-based scaling and plausible value methodology with full conditioning. The chapter reports gender differences in (i) interest-enjoyment in ICT, (ii) associations between interest-enjoyment and CIL by gender using correlations and effect sizes, and (iii) gender differences in patterns of ICT use (productivity applications, social communication, exchanging information, recreation, and study purposes) and their relationships with CIL using bivariate correlations and multiple regression models with country-specific fixed effects (country means of predictors set to zero within each country). Analyses are conducted on weighted data with sampling weights and nonresponse adjustments; however, the excerpt does not specify missing-data handling for questionnaire items. Overall, male students report higher interest-enjoyment and show stronger positive associations with CIL than female students, while gendered ICT-use patterns do not consistently translate into systematic advantages in CIL achievement.
